Since their inception in 1995, the Raptors have made the playoffs thirteen times (2000–2002, 2007, 2008, 2014–2020 and 2022), advancing past the first round six times (2001 and 2016–2020). The Raptors have won the Atlantic Division seven times (2007, 2014–2016, and 2018–2020), and the franchise record number of wins in the regular season is 59 (2018). The Raptors advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals twice (2016 and 2019). Only once did the Raptors reach and win the NBA Finals ([2019](/wiki/2019_NBA_Finals "2019 NBA Finals")). Honduras :: part 03 :: chunk_0002
**Honduras**,[[c]](#cite_note-10) officially the **Republic of Honduras**,[[d]](#cite_note-11) is a country in [Central America](/wiki/Central_America "Central America"). It is bordered to the west by [Guatemala](/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala"), to the southwest by [El Salvador](/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador"), to the southeast by [Nicaragua](/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua"), to the south by the [Pacific Ocean](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") at the [Gulf of Fonseca](/wiki/Gulf_of_Fonseca "Gulf of Fonseca"), and to the north by the [Gulf of Honduras](/wiki/Gulf_of_Honduras "Gulf of Honduras"), a large inlet of the [Caribbean Sea](/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"). Its [capital](/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and largest city is [Tegucigalpa](/wiki/Tegucigalpa "Tegucigalpa").

Honduras was home to several important [Mesoamerican](/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica") cultures, most notably the [Maya](/wiki/Maya_civilization "Maya civilization"), before [Spanish colonization](/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas "Spanish colonization of the Americas") in the sixteenth century. The Spanish introduced [Catholicism](/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") and the now-predominant [Spanish language](/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), along with numerous customs that have blended with the indigenous culture. Honduras became independent in 1821 and has since been a republic, although it has consistently endured much social strife and political instability, and remains one of the poorest countries in the [Western Hemisphere](/wiki/Western_Hemisphere "Western Hemisphere"). In 1960, the northern part of what was the [Mosquito Coast](/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast") was transferred from Nicaragua to Honduras by the [International Court of Justice](/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice").[[8]](#cite_note-auto-12)

The nation's economy is primarily [agricultural](/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"

Moon :: History of scientific understanding and exploration :: Renewed exploration (1990–present) :: part 01 :: chunk_0038
In 1990 *[Hiten](/wiki/Hiten_(spacecraft) "Hiten (spacecraft)")* – *Hagoromo*,[[281]](#cite_note-294) the first dedicated lunar mission since 1976, reached the Moon's orbit. Sent by Japan, it became the first lunar mission that was not a Soviet Union or U.S. mission.

In 1994, the U.S. dedicated a mission to fly a spacecraft (*[Clementine](/wiki/Clementine_(spacecraft) "Clementine (spacecraft)")*) to the Moon again for the first time since 1973. This mission obtained the first near-global topographic map of the Moon, and the first global [multispectral](/wiki/Multispectral "Multispectral") images of the lunar surface.[[282]](#cite_note-295) In 1998, this was followed by the *[Lunar Prospector](/wiki/Lunar_Prospector "Lunar Prospector")* mission, whose instruments indicated the presence of excess hydrogen at the lunar poles, which is likely to have been caused by the presence of water ice in the upper few meters of the regolith within permanently shadowed craters.[[283]](#cite_note-296)

The next years saw a row of first missions to the Moon by a new group of states actively exploring the Moon.
Between 2004 and 2006 the first spacecraft by the [European Space Agency](/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") (ESA) ([SMART-1](/wiki/SMART-1 "SMART-1")) orbited the Moon, recording the first detailed survey of chemical elements on the lunar surface.[[284]](#cite_note-297)
The [Chinese Lunar Exploration Program](/wiki/Chinese_Lunar_Exploration_Program "Chinese Lunar Exploration Program") reached the Moon for the first time with the orbiter *[Chang'e 1](/wiki/Chang%27e_1 "Chang'e 1")* (2007–2009),[[285]](#cite_note-298) obtaining a full image map of the Moon.

On August 11, 2015, Google announced plans to create a new public [holding company](/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company"), Alphabet Inc. Google co-founder and CEO [Larry Page](/wiki/Larry_Page "Larry Page") made this announcement in a blog post on Google's official blog.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Alphabet was created to restructure Google by moving subsidiaries from Google to Alphabet, thus narrowing Google's scope. The new holding company would consist of Google as well as other businesses including [X Development](/wiki/X_Development "X Development"), [Calico](/wiki/Calico_(company) "Calico (company)"), [Nest](/wiki/Google_Nest "Google Nest"), [Verily](/wiki/Verily "Verily"), [Fiber](/wiki/Google_Fiber "Google Fiber"), [CapitalG](/wiki/CapitalG "CapitalG"), and [GV](/wiki/GV_(company) "GV (company)").[[9]](#cite_note-bloomberg2015-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) [Sundar Pichai](/wiki/Sundar_Pichai "Sundar Pichai"), the company's Product Chief, became the new chief executive officer of Google, replacing Page, who transitioned to the role of running Alphabet, along with co-founder Sergey Brin.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-NYT_2015_Dougherty-13) Alphabet is the world's [second-largest technology company by revenue](/wiki/List_of_largest_technology_companies_by_revenue "List of largest technology companies by revenue"), after [Nvidia](/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia"), the largest technology company by profit, and the world's [most valuable companies](/wiki/List_of_public_corporations_by_market_capitalization "List of public corporations by market capitalization").[[14]](#cite_note-Fortune-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In his announcement, Page stated that the planned holding company would allow for "more management scale, as we can run things independently that aren't very related" to Google. List of largest cruise ships :: Timeline :: chunk_0001
The first large cruise ships were the [*Destiny*-class](/wiki/Destiny-class_cruise_ship "Destiny-class cruise ship") from [Carnival Cruise Line](/wiki/Carnival_Cruise_Line "Carnival Cruise Line"). The lead ship *Carnival Destiny* was the first to exceed 100,000 gross tons and the first to eclipse *RMS Queen Elizabeth* in terms of tonnage.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

*Grand Princess* eclipsed *Carnival Destiny* in 1998.

The [*Voyager*-class](/wiki/Voyager-class_cruise_ship "Voyager-class cruise ship") from [Royal Caribbean Group](/wiki/Royal_Caribbean_Group "Royal Caribbean Group")'s [Royal Caribbean International](/wiki/Royal_Caribbean_International "Royal Caribbean International") (RCI) debuted in 1998 and at over 137,000 GT, were almost 30,000 GT larger than the next-largest cruise ships, and were some of the first designed to offer amenities such as an [ice rink](/wiki/Ice_rink "Ice rink") and [climbing wall](/wiki/Climbing_wall "Climbing wall").[[1]](#cite_note-saunders-1)

In 2004, the five *Voyager*-class ships were overtaken by the 148,528 GT [*Queen Mary 2*](/wiki/Queen_Mary_2 "Queen Mary 2") (*QM2*), the only [ocean liner](/wiki/Ocean_liner "Ocean liner") currently in service.

*QM2* was surpassed by RCI's 155,889 GT [*Freedom*](/wiki/Freedom-class_cruise_ship "Freedom-class cruise ship")-class vessels in 2006, which were in turn overtaken by RCI's first of six planned [*Oasis*-class](/wiki/Oasis-class_cruise_ship "Oasis-class cruise ship") vessels in 2009.[[18]](#cite_note-RCIoasis6-18) The *Oasis*-class ships, at over 225,000 GT, at least 154 feet (47 m) wide, 240 feet (73 m) high, and 1,180 feet (360m) long, can accommodate over 5,400 passengers.[[19]](#cite_note-19) Oasis-class ships were surpassed by the first [*Icon*-class](/wiki/Icon-class_cruise_ship "Icon-class cruise ship") ship, [*Icon of the Seas*](/wiki/Icon_of_the_Seas "Icon of the Seas"), at 248,663 GT in 2023.

fanoutqa_009776.x:
University of Oxford :: Oxford in literature and popular media :: chunk_0032
The University of Oxford is the setting for numerous works of fiction. Oxford was mentioned in fiction as early as 1400 when [Chaucer](/wiki/Chaucer "Chaucer"), in *[Canterbury Tales](/wiki/Canterbury_Tales "Canterbury Tales")*, referred to a "Clerk [student] of Oxenford".[[235]](#cite_note-239) Mortimer Proctor argues the first campus novel was *The Adventures of Oxymel Classic, Esq; Once an Oxford Scholar* (1768).[[236]](#cite_note-240) It is filled with violence and debauchery, with obnoxious, foolish dons becoming easy prey for cunning students.[[237]](#cite_note-241) Proctor argues that by 1900, "novels about Oxford and Cambridge were so numerous that they clearly represent a striking literary phenomenon."[[238]](#cite_note-242) By 1989, 533 novels based in Oxford had been identified and the number continues to rise.[[239]](#cite_note-243)

Famous literary works range from *[Brideshead Revisited](/wiki/Brideshead_Revisited "Brideshead Revisited")* by [Evelyn Waugh](/wiki/Evelyn_Waugh "Evelyn Waugh"), which in 1981 was adapted as a [television serial](/wiki/Brideshead_Revisited_(TV_serial) "Brideshead Revisited (TV serial)"), to the trilogy *[His Dark Materials](/wiki/His_Dark_Materials "His Dark Materials")* by [Philip Pullman](/wiki/Philip_Pullman "Philip Pullman"), which features an alternate-reality version of the university and was adapted for [film in 2007](/wiki/The_Golden_Compass_(film) "The Golden Compass (film)") and as a [BBC television series in 2019](/wiki/His_Dark_Materials_(TV_series) "His Dark Materials (TV series)").

Other notable examples include:

* *[Zuleika Dobson](/wiki/Zuleika_Dobson "Zuleika Dobson")* (1911) by [Max Beerbohm](/wiki/Max_Beerbohm "Max Beerbohm"), a satire about undergraduate life.
* *[Gaudy Night](/wiki/Gaudy_Night "Gaudy Night")* (1935) by [Dorothy L. Sayers](/wiki/Dorothy_L._Sayers "Dorothy L. Sayers"), herself a graduate of [Somerville College]

Ko Wen-je :: Mayor of Taipei (2014–2022) :: Emergency preparedness :: chunk_0009
Ko built two [detention basins](/wiki/Detention_basin "Detention basin") in the [Wenshan district](/wiki/Wenshan_District "Wenshan District") to help prevent [flash floods](/wiki/Flash_flood "Flash flood").[[75]](#cite_note-:8-79)[[76]](#cite_note-:9-80) Construction on both started in November 2015.[[75]](#cite_note-:8-79) By October 2017, both detention basins were operational with a combined volume of 45,000 cubic meters.[[76]](#cite_note-:9-80) According to Ko, with the new detention basins contributing to a comprehensive flood control strategy, the area could now withstand up to 78.8 millimeters per hour of rain without flooding, up from 59 mm per hour previously, bringing Wenshan district up to the same standards as the rest of Taipei.[[75]](#cite_note-:8-79)[[76]](#cite_note-:9-80)

Figures for the **population of Europe** vary according to the particular [definition of Europe's boundaries](/wiki/Europe#Definition "Europe"). In 2018, Europe had a total population of over 745 million people.[[1]](#cite_note-UN_WPP-1)[[2]](#cite_note-UN_WPP_2022-2) Around 448 million of them lived in the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and around 110 million in [European Russia](/wiki/European_Russia "European Russia"); Russia is the [most populous country](/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_population "List of European countries by population") in Europe.

Europe's [population growth](/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth") is low, and its [median age](/wiki/Population_pyramid "Population pyramid") high. Most of Europe is in a mode of [sub-replacement fertility](/wiki/Sub-replacement_fertility "Sub-replacement fertility"), which means that each new(-born) generation is less populous than the one before.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Nonetheless, most West European countries still have growing populations, mainly due to [immigration](/wiki/Immigration "Immigration") within Europe and from outside Europe and some due to increases in [life expectancy](/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") and [population momentum](/wiki/Population_momentum

By the end of 2015 a total of 8,745 [wildfires](/wiki/Wildfire "Wildfire") were recorded across the state of [California](/wiki/California "California"), burning 893,362 acres (3,615 km2).[[1]](#cite_note-NIFC-1) Approximately 3,159 structures were damaged or destroyed by wildfires, and at least 7 fatalities were recorded.

On September 11, after the [Butte Fire](/wiki/Butte_Fire "Butte Fire") exploded from a size of 32,000 acres (129 km2)[[4]](#cite_note-nbc-warning-4) to 65,000 acres (263 km2), in the [Amador](/wiki/Amador_County,_California "Amador County, California") and [Calaveras](/wiki/Calaveras_County,_California "Calaveras County, California") counties, [Governor Jerry Brown](/wiki/Governor_Jerry_Brown "Governor Jerry Brown") declared a [state of emergency](/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency").[[5]](#cite_note-soe-5)
